text: 70 million liters of hot water rise under Budapest every day,
and you'd never guess what it's doing down there.
So, where does all that hot water come from?
Here, Earth's crust is thin.
It heats up about one degree every 20 meters down.
Rain sinks deep into the Buddha Hills,
heats up, and rises back through a fault line.
Result, 123 hot springs and wells.
But that's not the strange part.
The Romans built 14 baths here. The Ottomans added more, still open nearly 500 years later.
Some regulars looked like they never got out.
But the water wasn't just warming people, it was eating rock.
Most caves are dug by rain from above. These were dug by hot water from below.
So what's down there now?
Behind a metal door near a busy road, a flooded cave, about 6 kilometers long.
Divers swim through it in warm water under a hill full of houses.
No traffic down there. Best commute in Budapest.
Down there, fossil shark teeth, in hungry, which has no sea, now.
Budapest doesn't just have hot springs, it's sitting on one.
And the twist? That cave is still growing.
Right now, hot water is still dissolving the rock.
Very, very slowly.
This is Boogal. Follow for more geography fun facts.
